title: Missing -s after he/she/it
wrong: My sister **work** in a bank.
right: My sister **works** in a bank.
why: English verbs change with a third-person singular subject in the present; Vietnamese verbs never change.

title: Missing verb *be* before an adjective
wrong: This city **very** crowded.
right: This city **is** very crowded.
why: An English sentence needs a verb. Adjectives cannot be the verb, so use *be*.

title: *be* + base verb
wrong: I **am agree** with this view.
right: I **agree** with this view.
why: *agree* is already a verb; don't add *be*.

title: Stative verb in -ing
wrong: I **am knowing** the answer.
right: I **know** the answer.
why: Verbs of knowing, liking and owning are rarely used in the progressive.

title: No past marking
wrong: Last summer I **work** at a café.
right: Last summer I **worked** at a café.
why: A finished past time needs a past verb form, even when the time word is already there.
viCue: time word does the job in Vietnamese

title: *đã* → present perfect with a finished time
wrong: I **have visited** Huế **in 2023**.
right: I **visited** Huế in 2023.
why: With a finished time (*in 2023, last week, ago*), use the simple past.

title: Simple present for "since/for"
wrong: I **live** here **since** 2020.
right: I **have lived** here since 2020.
why: An action that started in the past and continues now takes the present perfect.

title: Irregular past as regular
wrong: She **teached** us maths.
right: She **taught** us maths.
why: Irregular verbs have their own past forms; check the reference table.

title: *will* after *when/if* for the future
wrong: **When** I **will finish** school, I will study abroad.
right: **When** I **finish** school, I will study abroad.
why: In time and *if* clauses about the future, use the present.

title: Tense jumping in a story
wrong: Yesterday I went to the library and I **see** my teacher.
right: Yesterday I went to the library and I **saw** my teacher.
why: Keep one time frame unless a time word signals a shift.

title: *people* + singular verb
wrong: Many people **is** worried about pollution.
right: Many people **are** worried about pollution.
why: *people* is plural.

title: Verb agrees with the nearest noun
wrong: The quality of the roads **are** poor.
right: The quality of the roads **is** poor.
why: The verb agrees with the head noun (*quality*), not the noun just before it.

title: *There have* for existence
wrong: **There have** many parks in Đà Nẵng.
right: **There are** many parks in Đà Nẵng.
why: For existence, English uses *there is/are*, not *have*.

title: Modal + to / + -s / + -ed
wrong: Students **should to** read more. / She **cans** swim.
right: Students **should** read more. / She **can** swim.
why: A modal is followed by the base verb, and never takes -s.

title: *must* for all advice
wrong: You **must** try the street food.
right: You **should** try the street food.
why: *must* is strong obligation; use *should* for advice.

title: Passive with intransitive verbs
wrong: The accident **was happened** at night.
right: The accident **happened** at night.
why: Verbs without an object (*happen, occur, arrive*) have no passive.

title: Active form where passive is needed
wrong: This bridge **built** in 1990.
right: This bridge **was built** in 1990.
why: When the subject receives the action, use *be* + past participle.

title: *make/let* + to
wrong: This game **makes me to feel** relaxed.
right: This game **makes me feel** relaxed.
why: *make, let, have* + object + base verb.

title: *suggest* + object + to
wrong: My teacher **suggested me to join** the club.
right: My teacher **suggested (that) I join** / **suggested joining** the club.
why: *suggest* is not followed by object + infinitive.

title: *to* as preposition + base verb
wrong: I look forward to **hear** from you.
right: I look forward to **hearing** from you.
why: After a preposition (*to* in *look forward to*), use *-ing*.

title: Past modal without *have*
wrong: The delay **might been** caused by the rain.
right: The delay **might have been** caused by the rain.
why: A past modal is modal + *have* + past participle.

title: Two modals in a row
wrong: We **will can** finish the report next week.
right: We **will be able to** finish the report next week.
why: English allows one modal per verb phrase; use a phrasal modal for the second idea.

title: *must* used as a past form
wrong: She **musted** leave early yesterday.
right: She **had to** leave early yesterday.
why: *must* has no past form; use *had to* for past obligation.

title: Passive *be* does not agree with the new subject
wrong: The results **has been** shown to the head teacher.
right: The results **have been** shown to the head teacher.
why: In a passive, *be* agrees with the subject, which is often plural after the change.

title: Base verb after *be* in a passive
wrong: The labels should **be print** before Friday.
right: The labels should **be printed** before Friday.
why: A passive always takes the past participle, never the base form.

title: *want / would like* + *that*-clause
wrong: My parents **want that I study** medicine.
right: My parents **want me to study** medicine.
why: *want* and *would like* take an object + infinitive, not a *that*-clause.

title: *be used to* + base verb
wrong: I **am used to get** up at five.
right: I **am used to getting** up at five.
why: The *to* in *be/get used to* is a preposition, so it takes *-ing*; *used to* + base verb is the different, past-habit pattern.

title: *used to* + past verb
wrong: I **used to played** badminton after school.
right: I **used to play** badminton after school.
why: *used to* is always followed by the base verb.

title: Double past marking after *did*
wrong: We **didn't knew** the answer.
right: We **didn't know** the answer.
why: After *did* or *didn't*, the main verb goes back to its base form.

title: *would* for a past state
wrong: My uncle **would have** a small restaurant near the market.
right: My uncle **used to have** a small restaurant near the market.
why: *would* only describes repeated past actions; states take *used to* or the simple past.

title: Future perfect with a base verb
wrong: I **will have finish** the report by June.
right: I **will have finished** the report by June.
why: After *have*, use the past participle.

title: *Since* + simple past for a period up to now
wrong: **Since 2019 the school opened** three new clubs.
right: **Since 2019 the school has opened** three new clubs.
why: A period that runs up to now takes the present perfect, not the simple past.

title: Gerund subject with a plural verb
wrong: **Learning two languages take** time and patience.
right: **Learning two languages takes** time and patience.
why: An *-ing* subject is singular, however many nouns follow it.

title: *neither … nor* agreement
wrong: Neither my father nor my uncle **drive** a car.
right: Neither my father nor my uncle **drives** a car.
why: With *either… or* and *neither… nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

title: Plural of uncountable nouns
wrong: She gave me some useful **advices** / **informations**.
right: She gave me some useful **advice** / **information**.
why: Some nouns are uncountable in English even if they are countable ideas in Vietnamese.

title: No plural after a number or *many*
wrong: There are three **student** in my group.
right: There are three **students** in my group.
why: Count nouns need -s after numbers above one and after *many, several, a few*.

title: *much* with count nouns
wrong: There are **much** problems in big cities.
right: There are **many** problems in big cities.
why: *many* + plural count nouns; *much* + uncountable nouns.

title: Missing article with a singular count noun
wrong: My father is **doctor**.
right: My father is **a doctor**.
why: A singular count noun needs a determiner (*a, the, my…*).

title: *the* with general plural/uncountable nouns
wrong: **The** pollution is a serious problem.
right: Pollution is a serious problem.
why: For things in general, use no article with plural and uncountable nouns.

title: Missing *the* for known/unique things
wrong: **Government** should build more schools. / I went to **cinema**.
right: **The government** should… / I went to **the cinema**.
why: Use *the* when the reader knows which one.

title: Dropped subject *it*
wrong: **Is** important to protect the environment.
right: **It is** important to protect the environment.
why: English sentences need a subject, even a dummy *it*.

title: *he/she* mix-up
wrong: My mother is a nurse. **He** works at night.
right: My mother is a nurse. **She** works at night.
why: English pronouns mark gender; check the noun they refer to.
viCue: spoken *nó / anh ấy / chị ấy* habits

title: Double subject
wrong: My brother **he** plays football.
right: My brother plays football.
why: Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun.

title: Plural verb with an academic uncountable noun
wrong: The research **are** limited and her advice **were** practical.
right: The research **is** limited and her advice **was** practical.
why: *research, advice, evidence, information* are uncountable, so they take a singular verb.

title: Demonstrative does not match the number of the noun
wrong: I bought **this two books** before **these trip**.
right: I bought **these two books** before **this trip**.
why: *this/that* go with singular nouns; *these/those* go with plural ones.

title: Possessive determiner and possessive pronoun swapped
wrong: This bag is not **my**. It is **hers bag**.
right: This bag is not **mine**. It is **her bag**.
why: *my, her, their* need a noun after them; *mine, hers, theirs* stand alone.

title: Comma splice
wrong: Traffic is heavy, many people are late for work.
right: Traffic is heavy, **so** many people are late for work. / …heavy**.** Many…
why: Two full sentences need a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction, not only a comma.

title: Fragment with *Because*
wrong: I stayed at home. **Because it was raining.**
right: I stayed at home **because** it was raining.
why: A *because* clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.

title: *Although … but*
wrong: **Although** it was late, **but** we kept working.
right: **Although** it was late, we kept working.
why: Use one linking word per contrast: *although* **or** *but*.

title: *Because … so*
wrong: **Because** the fee is high, **so** few people join.
right: **Because** the fee is high, few people join.
why: Use *because* **or** *so*, not both.

title: Non-parallel list
wrong: I like reading, **to swim** and **go** hiking.
right: I like reading, swimming and hiking.
why: Items in a list take the same form.

title: *which* for people
wrong: The teacher **which** helped me is retiring.
right: The teacher **who** helped me is retiring.
why: *who* for people, *which* for things.

title: Extra pronoun in a relative clause
wrong: This is the book **that** I bought **it** yesterday.
right: This is the book that I bought yesterday.
why: The relative pronoun replaces the object; don't repeat it.

title: *will* in the *if* clause
wrong: **If** it **will rain**, we will cancel the trip.
right: **If** it **rains**, we will cancel the trip.
why: Real future conditionals: present in the *if* clause.

title: Past hypothetical with the wrong form
wrong: If I **studied** harder last year, I **would pass**.
right: If I **had studied** harder last year, I **would have passed**.
why: For unreal past situations: *had* + past participle / *would have* + past participle.

title: *Which* clause left as its own sentence
wrong: The bus was late. **Which made** us miss the first talk.
right: The bus was late, **which made** us miss the first talk.
why: A *which* clause commenting on a whole sentence stays attached to it with a comma; alone it is a fragment.
viCue: *điều đó / cái mà* started as a new sentence

title: Doubled possessive after *whose*
wrong: I have a friend **whose her father** runs a bakery.
right: I have a friend **whose father** runs a bakery.
why: *whose* already carries the possessive, so *her/his/their* repeats it.

title: *Despite / In spite of* + clause
wrong: **Despite the shop was small**, it sold everything we needed.
right: **Although the shop was small**, it sold everything we needed. / **Despite its small size**, it sold…
why: *despite* and *in spite of* are prepositions and take a noun or *-ing*; a clause needs *although*.

title: Double negative after *unless*
wrong: **Unless you don't book** early, the tickets will sell out.
right: **Unless you book** early, the tickets will sell out.
why: *unless* already means *if… not*, so a second negative reverses the meaning.

title: Run-on sentence with no mark between clauses
wrong: My uncle drives a lorry **he leaves** before dawn.
right: My uncle drives a lorry**, and he leaves** before dawn.
why: Two complete sentences need a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction.
viCue: Vietnamese can chain clauses with no mark

title: *-ed / -ing* adjectives
wrong: I am very **interesting** in history.
right: I am very **interested** in history.
why: *-ed* = how you feel; *-ing* = what causes the feeling.

title: Noun instead of adjective
wrong: This is a very **success** project.
right: This is a very **successful** project.
why: Before a noun, use the adjective form.

title: Adjective instead of adverb
wrong: She speaks English very **fluent**.
right: She speaks English very **fluently**.
why: Use an adverb to describe a verb.

title: *economic / economical*
wrong: Buses are an **economic** way to travel.
right: Buses are an **economical** way to travel.
why: *economic* = about the economy; *economical* = saving money.

title: *rise / raise*
wrong: The government plans to **rise** taxes.
right: The government plans to **raise** taxes.
why: *raise* takes an object; *rise* does not.

title: *lose / miss*
wrong: I **lost** the bus this morning.
right: I **missed** the bus this morning.
why: You *miss* a bus, class or chance; you *lose* an object.

title: Extra preposition
wrong: We **discussed about** the plan. / She **married with** him.
right: We **discussed** the plan. / She **married** him.
why: Some verbs take a direct object with no preposition.

title: Wrong dependent preposition
wrong: He is good **in** maths. / It depends **of** the weather.
right: He is good **at** maths. / It depends **on** the weather.
why: Many adjectives and verbs take a fixed preposition; learn them as chunks.

title: *in/on/at* with time
wrong: See you **on** 7 p.m. **in** Monday.
right: See you **at** 7 p.m. **on** Monday.
why: *at* + clock time, *on* + day/date, *in* + month/year/part of day.

title: *In my opinion, I think*
wrong: **In my opinion, I think** fees should be lower.
right: **In my opinion,** fees should be lower. / **I think** fees…
why: Both mean the same thing; use one.

title: their / there / they're
wrong: **Their** are many reasons to cycle to school.
right: **There** are many reasons to cycle to school.
why: *There* introduces something that exists, *their* shows possession, and *they're* is short for *they are*.
viCue: *họ / có* — the three English words sound identical

title: its / it's
wrong: The city lost **it's** old trees.
right: The city lost **its** old trees.
why: The apostrophe in *it's* stands for the missing letter of *is*, never for possession.

title: affect / effect
wrong: The new rule will **effect** every class.
right: The new rule will **affect** every class.
why: *Affect* is the verb; *effect* is almost always the noun (*have an effect on*).

title: than / then
wrong: Huế is quieter **then** Đà Nẵng.
right: Huế is quieter **than** Đà Nẵng.
why: *Than* follows a comparative; *then* means *after that*.

title: advice / advise
wrong: She **adviced** me to apply early.
right: She **advised** me to apply early.
why: *Advice* is the uncountable noun; *advise* is the verb, so it takes -d in the past.

title: in / on / at with place
wrong: I waited **on** the bus stop **in** the corner of the street.
right: I waited **at** the bus stop **on** the corner of the street.
why: *At* for a point, *on* for a surface or a line, *in* for an enclosed space.
